# codex's surface, read off the binary

Everything the pinned `codex` will say about itself, captured by
`scripts/codex-surface.sh` and regenerated on demand by
`.github/workflows/codex-surface.yml` (`workflow_dispatch` only, no
schedule, no credential). It is `docs/agy-surface.md`'s counterpart for
the other CLI `pkg/agent` drives, and it exists for one question that
document cannot answer: which flags codex takes at the top level, and
which it takes only under `exec`.

That question has two answers in this repository, because `pkg/agent/codex`
builds two different command lines -- `codex exec --json
--skip-git-repo-check ...` for an unattended run, and a bare `codex ...`
for an interactive session somebody types into (`terminal.go`) -- and
until this capture existed, the second one was asserted against no binary
at all. The first run of this script is what found `--skip-git-repo-check`
on the wrong side of that line.

Read it as evidence rather than as documentation: every section below is a
command and its output, the commands that failed included. A probe that
stopped answering is itself a finding.

Unlike agy, codex is pinned here: the Dockerfile names a release
(`ARG CODEX_CLI_VERSION`), the workflow installs that release rather than
the latest, and `pkg/agent/codex/surface_capture_test.go` fails when the
pin moves and this file does not -- so "the capture is old" is a question
this document can answer about itself.

## The binary

``````console
$ codex --version
codex-cli 0.153.0
``````

``````console
path   /opt/codex/codex-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
size   258471008 bytes
sha256 fce635028842bfe9257140e8b7d53162732945e2f356fc35225be0702b4974be
``````

The release this capture is of, against the release the image carries:

``````console
pinned by the Dockerfile   rust-v0.153.0
captured here              codex-cli 0.153.0
``````

And one line codex prints ahead of almost everything, which every capture below has had removed from it and which is worth reading once. Every probe in this document runs with a `CODEX_HOME` under `/tmp`, because that is what `writeConfig` gives a real run -- `os.MkdirTemp("")` -- so this is what a grain run gets too:

``````console
WARNING: proceeding, even though we could not create PATH aliases: Refusing to create helper binaries under temporary dir "/tmp" (codex_home: AbsolutePathBuf("$PROBE/home-1"))
``````

          Intended only for automation that already vets hook sources

          Intended only for automation that already vets hook sources

  -C, --cd <DIR>

  -a, --ask-for-approval <APPROVAL_POLICY>

          Possible values:
          - on-request: The model decides when to ask the user for approval
          - never:      Never ask for user approval Execution failures are immediately returned to
            the model

      --search
          Enable live web search. When enabled, the native Responses `web_search` tool is available
          to the model (no per‑call approval)

      --no-alt-screen
          Disable alternate screen mode
          
          Runs the TUI in inline mode, preserving terminal scrollback history.

## Where each flag lives

The two listings above, read as sets. `codex` and `codex exec` are separate clap commands with separate flag sets, and a flag in one is not a flag in the other -- which is the single fact this whole document was added to record. `both` means the name is accepted in both positions; it does not mean it does the same thing in each.

``````console
$ which command each long flag belongs to
both           --add-dir
both           --approve-for-me
both           --cd
both           --config
both           --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
both           --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust
both           --disable
both           --enable
both           --help
both           --image
both           --last
both           --local-provider
both           --model
both           --oss
both           --profile
both           --sandbox
both           --strict-config
both           --version
exec only      --color
exec only      --ephemeral
exec only      --ignore-rules
exec only      --ignore-user-config
exec only      --json
exec only      --output-last-message
exec only      --output-schema
exec only      --skip-git-repo-check
exec only      --thread-source
top-level only --ask-for-approval
top-level only --no-alt-screen
top-level only --remote
top-level only --remote-auth-token-env
top-level only --search
``````

## The argv grain builds

The listings above are what codex says. This section is what it does, asked one flag at a time and at the exact position `pkg/agent/codex` puts it: `codexArgs` for an unattended run, `TerminalCommand` for a session. Each row appends `--help` so that nothing runs -- clap parses the whole argv before it acts on `--help`, so an unrecognized argument is still an error and a recognized one still exits 0.

`accepted` here means the flag is spelled and positioned correctly. It is not a claim about the value: codex resolves neither a model name nor a path while parsing.

This list is the one place in this document that names flags rather than discovering them, and `pkg/agent/codex/surface_capture_test.go` is what keeps it honest: a flag that package passes and this script does not probe fails that test rather than going unmeasured.

``````console
$ does this codex accept the flag at that position
rejected  top-level  --skip-git-repo-check    error: unexpected argument '--skip-git-repo-check' found
rejected  top-level  --json                   error: unexpected argument '--json' found
accepted  top-level  --model
accepted  exec       --skip-git-repo-check
accepted  exec       --json
accepted  exec       --model
``````

And the two argv whole, since a flag set that parses one flag at a time can still be refused together. The unattended one is shown without its trailing `-` -- the positional that tells codex to read the prompt from stdin, which `--help` would make meaningless -- and the session one is exactly what `TerminalCommand` returns.

``````console
$ does this codex accept the whole command line
accepted  codex exec --json --skip-git-repo-check --model gpt-5-codex --help
          the unattended run: codexArgs, minus the stdin positional
accepted  codex --model gpt-5-codex --help
          the session: TerminalCommand
``````

## Interactive mode

What `codex` does with no subcommand at all, which is what `TerminalCommand` runs. Its own `--help` opens by saying it: "If no subcommand is specified, options will be forwarded to the interactive CLI."

First, without a terminal. Both probes below run in a directory that is not a git repository -- the case a granule run is always in, since it has no local directory and leaves codex started wherever the daemon happens to be.

``````console
$ codex
ERROR: TERM is set to "dumb". Refusing to start the interactive TUI because no terminal is available for a confirmation prompt (stdin/stderr is not a TTY). Run in a supported terminal or unset TERM.
[exit 1]
``````

The same thing inside a git repository, so that the message above can be read for what it is about:

``````console
$ codex
ERROR: TERM is set to "dumb". Refusing to start the interactive TUI because no terminal is available for a confirmation prompt (stdin/stderr is not a TTY). Run in a supported terminal or unset TERM.
[exit 1]
``````

A refusal about the terminal rather than about the repository, in both. codex `exec` is the half of this binary that refuses to start outside a git repository ("Not inside a trusted directory and --skip-git-repo-check was not specified"), and it is the half that has a `--skip-git-repo-check` to be told otherwise with.

So what does the interactive half do about a directory it does not trust? It asks. Below is the TUI started on a pty in each case, with a credential planted so the login screen is not what gets captured -- a word list rather than a screen, for the reason `tui_fragments` gives in the script.

### The TUI in a directory it has not been told to trust

``````console
$ codex --no-alt-screen, on a pty, in a directory that is not a repository
$PROBE/home-1
$PROBE/plain-1
Ask Codex to do anything
OpenAI Codex
Press enter to continue
Trusting
Working
Yes, continue
You are in
allows
and
codex
comes
config,
contents
directory
directory:
directory?
exec
for shortcuts
helper binaries under temporary dir
higher
home: AbsolutePathBuf(
hooks,
injection.
load.
loading
model
model:
policies
project-local
prompt
quit
risk
the
this
tmp
to change
trust
untrusted
with
you
``````

### The same, with that directory pre-trusted in `config.toml`

codex records a decision like that under `[projects."<path>"] trust_level`, which is a thing `writeConfig` could write and does not. This is what it would buy.

``````console
$ phrase                       untrusted    trust_level = "trusted"
trust                        drawn        not drawn
untrusted                    drawn        not drawn
Yes, continue                drawn        not drawn
Ask Codex to do anything     drawn        drawn
``````

The trust question is gone in the second column and the prompt is there in both, which is the whole finding: an interactive codex started outside a repository asks the person who opened the session, and takes an answer. Nothing on that command line can pre-empt the question -- `--skip-git-repo-check` is `exec`'s, as the table above records -- but `config.toml` can, and the session shares its `CODEX_HOME` with the run.

The slash commands a session gets, which is half of what somebody opens one for, are not in this document: they are typed into that TUI rather than printed by any probe. `codex --help` lists no flag that disables them, which is the only claim `terminal.go` needs from here.

## What it loads out of the config grain writes

A session and an unattended run of the same task share one `CODEX_HOME`, written by `writeConfig`, and everything that decides what either may reach is in it rather than on the command line. This section reads that file back through codex itself.

The file, as `configTOML` builds it (copied into this script, and diffable against that function by eye):

``````toml
# Written by grain for one run; see pkg/agent/codex.
approval_policy = "never"
sandbox_mode = "read-only"

[features]
code_mode_host = false

[mcp_servers.grain]
command = "/bin/true"
args = []
``````

``````console
$ codex mcp list
Name   Command    Args  Env  Cwd  Status   Auth       
grain  /bin/true  -     -    -    enabled  Unsupported
``````

``````console
$ codex --strict-config mcp list
Error: `--strict-config` is not supported for `codex mcp`
[exit 1]
``````

`--strict-config` is the interesting one: it makes codex error on a key it does not recognize, which turns "grain writes a key that is silently ignored" from a thing nobody could see into a non-zero exit. It is not passed in production -- an unattended run must not die over a config key -- so this probe is where that answer lives.

## The keys, out of the string table

codex is a stripped release build, but a Rust binary carries every serde field name and every literal path its own code names. These are the keys `pkg/agent/codex` writes, looked for one at a time -- a name that stops appearing here is a key a new codex has renamed, and a config file full of them loads without complaint.

``````console
$ each name pkg/agent/codex depends on, in the binary's own strings
present                  approval_policy
present                  sandbox_mode
present                  mcp_servers
present                  code_mode_host
present                  trust_level
present                  projects
present                  config.toml
present                  auth.json
present                  CODEX_HOME
``````

And what codex itself will print about the repository check, which is where the flag this document is about actually lives. A Rust string table has no separators between its entries, so this is a fixed window around the match rather than a sentence:

``````console
$ strings -n 4 codex | grep -aoE '.{0,60}trusted directory.{0,60}'
ptForking with output options requires a promptNot inside a trusted directory and --skip-git-repo-check was not specified.
``````
